narrative:
The model estimates an 85% probability that you will leave your job. In practical terms, the organization has treated you as a likely near-term leaver, and that is why the promotion was denied: advancement is being reserved for employees expected to stay and grow here.

The strongest reason was your overall career experience. At 6–10 years, you are in a mid-career group that is less common among employees predicted to stay (about 35% of them), and this factor pushed the prediction toward leaving. The second-strongest factor was your shorter time in the current organization: 1–5 years, which also leaned toward leaving, even though it is common among stayers (about 51%). The third factor was that you reported other job opportunities; only about 23% of predicted stayers said they had such options, so this clearly pushed toward leaving.

These signals are reinforced by low job satisfaction, low emotional commitment, no recognition, no job stability, limited support, no bonus or medical insurance, no useful training, overtime, and feeling you did not get the promotion you deserved.

Before finalizing the decision, the organization should discuss whether these concerns can be addressed through clearer career progression, fair rewards, recognition, support, training, and work-life balance. You should also consider whether an internal move or retention plan would make staying worthwhile; otherwise, plan a constructive transition.
